questions: Does the oval still finish 20/20 near 1.65 s with the 8 mm footprint, or does the finer signal add oscillation?
On the s-bend and slalom, at what progress and lateral error does the first line loss start, and do the outer sensors read near 1 or near 0 at that step?
Does the 8 mm footprint make the sensor readings more binary, with more steps where the total reading falls below 0.05 or the signal jumps between sensors?
Compared with the 12 mm baseline, does steering oscillation rise or fall on the oval?

intent: Single-variable test against the iteration-0 baseline: keep every geometry value identical and reduce the sensor footprint from 12 mm to 8 mm to test whether finer edge resolution helps the s-bend and slalom without losing oval stability. Expected: oval finishes stay at about 20/20 with mean time near 1.65 s, and s-bend and slalom progress rises above 0.17 and 0.12.
learning: Iterations 1 to 4 show the oval is sensitive to sensor lead (y=0.03 and y=0.07 both collapse it) and to mass and drivetrain changes. The bend failures are not fixed by spread or lead alone, so the next lever to test is sensing resolution, which this iteration does with a single change. If the 8 mm footprint helps the bends without hurting the oval, combine it with a modest spread increase at 0.6 kg. If it does not, test 16 mm next.
rationale: Race evidence: the iteration-0 baseline (0.6 kg, 0.12 m track, 0.03 m radius, five sensors at ±0.024 m on a 12 mm pitch, y=0.05 m, 12 mm footprint) is still the best design at 356.6. It finishes the oval 20/20 in about 1.65 s but goes off track on the s-bend (progress 0.17) and slalom (progress 0.12). Every change since then has hurt. Widening the array and narrowing the track or lightening the robot (iterations 1 and 2) cut oval finishes to 17/20 and 15/20. Moving the sensors forward to y=0.07 m (iteration 3) collapsed the oval to 0/20. Moving them back to y=0.03 m (iteration 4) also collapsed the oval to 0/20 and scored only 118.9. So the oval is very sensitive to sensor lead, and y=0.05 m is a tight optimum. Iteration 4 also shows that the bend failures were not fixed by a shorter lead, so the remaining untested lever on the bends is sensor sensing resolution. This iteration therefore returns to the baseline body, drivetrain, array spread, pitch and lead exactly, and changes only the sensor footprint from 12 mm to 8 mm. Each sensor then sees a smaller patch, so the edge of the tape is resolved more sharply and the signal may track the line more precisely at the bends. Coverage is not lost: with the 12 mm pitch, the 25 mm tape always covers at least one sensor, so gaps between footprints do not drop the sum below 0.05. Expected result: the oval stays near 20/20 at about 1.65 s, and s-bend and slalom progress rises above 0.17 and 0.12. Risk: smaller footprints give a more binary, noisier signal, so steering oscillation may rise. If the oval falls, the 12 mm footprint stays the better choice and the next test should be a larger footprint (16 mm) with the same spread.
